checks.claim: Key: a muscle cell cannot live alone because it has no blood bringing it food and oxygen; cells of a many-celled body depend on the others and would not survive as independent cells
Context: blood pumped by the heart brings cells oxygen and nutrients; capillaries form a rich network around each muscle fibre
Wrong choice 'no nucleus': a skeletal (arm) muscle fibre is multinucleated
Wrong choice 'no mitochondria': muscle fibres hold thousands of mitochondria
Wrong choice 'no membrane': each fibre has a plasma membrane, the sarcolemma
Stem/context: an amoeba, a single cell, does every job of life by itself
Key: yeasts are single-celled fungi
Stem: wild yeasts live in soil and on the surfaces of plants and fruits; cells about 3-4 micrometres, far too small to see
Wrong choice 'bacterium': yeast is a eukaryote with a defined nucleus (context line 'each yeast cell has a nucleus')
Wrong choice 'alga': yeasts lack chlorophyll and are heterotrophs that cannot make their own food
Wrong choice 'one-celled animal' / context 'no animal is made of only one cell': all animals are multicellular; one-celled protozoa were removed from Animalia in the 19th century
Context: yeast is kin to mushrooms and moulds (same kingdom); yeasts mostly live as single cells (some form limited pseudohyphae, which does not change the answer)
Stem: some human cells are up to a metre long, from the lower back down the leg to the foot (axons of the sciatic nerve)
checks.note: Grokipedia: up to 1 metre, sciatic nerve, spinal cord to the foot. Wikipedia says 'one meter or more' and runs them from the base of the spinal cord to the big toe; 'up to a metre' is a fair grade-6 figure.

checks.claim: Key: these long cells (nerve cells) carry signals
Wrong choice 'shortens to pull on the bones': no muscle fibre is near a metre long
checks.note: Even the highest estimates for the longest fibres (sartorius) are about half a metre, so the lure stays wrong.

checks.claim: Context: 'even the longest [muscle cell] is under a third of a metre'
checks.note: Sources disagree, so the exact bound is not safe. OpenStax gives up to 30 cm, but anatomy sources (Folia Morphologica 2014, Physiopedia) estimate single sartorius fibres at 35-45 cm, and the 2005 J. Neuroscience study 'Muscle fiber and motor unit behavior in the longest human skeletal muscle' found at least 30% of motor units had fibres running virtually the full length of a muscle over 500 mm long. Fix: 'but even the longest falls far short of a metre'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'carries blood down to the foot' / context: blood flows in vessels built of many cells
Wrong choice 'holds the leg's bones together' / context: ligaments join bone to bone
Stem: a human red blood cell, maturing in the bone marrow, pushes out its nucleus and most other parts (the stem says human, so nucleated bird red cells do not clash)
checks.note: Grokipedia: in mammals 'the nucleus and most organelles, including mitochondria and ribosomes, are extruded'; the last ribosomal remnants go in the reticulocyte stage after release. Birds and other non-mammals keep nucleated red cells; the stem says human, so it is safe.

checks.claim: Key: losing them gives more room to carry oxygen (more space for haemoglobin)
checks.note: Grokipedia also names greater deformability as a gain; that is not among the wrong choices.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'divide faster': with no DNA a mature red cell cannot divide
Wrong choice 'longer life' / context 'lives only about four months': lifespan about 100-120 days, limited by no repair
Wrong choice 'tougher, stiffer outer wall' / context: no cell wall, a flexible disc that squeezes through capillaries as narrow as 3 micrometres
Context: haemoglobin is the protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to the body
Stem: Euglena is a single cell with a red eyespot that swims with a whip-like flagellum
checks.note: One long emergent flagellum (plus a short one that stays inside the cell).

checks.claim: Key: swimming to light suggests it makes its own food like a plant; phototaxis 'optimizes positioning for photosynthesis' with chlorophyll a and b chloroplasts
checks.note: Grokipedia notes very strong light reverses the response; a jar by a window in the stem is the classic classroom result, so the scenario stands.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'hunts by sight': the eyespot only shades a photoreceptor to sense light direction, forms no image; engulfing prey is rare in Euglena and never by sight
checks.note: Wikipedia: the eyespot itself is not thought to be photosensitive; it shades the light-sensing swelling at the flagellum base.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'seeks warmth': no documented thermotaxis in Euglena; the light response is phototaxis
Wrong choice 'follows the others': each cell senses light direction itself as it rotates
Context: in the dark Euglena can take in food from the water instead (osmotrophy on dissolved organics)
checks.note: The context calls it 'an autotroph, like a plant' and then gives the dark feeding, so the mixotroph fact is told honestly.

checks.claim: Stem: a Venus flytrap 'snaps two leaves shut' on a fly
checks.note: Each trap is ONE leaf: Grokipedia 'modified terminal leaves divided into two hinged lobes'; Wikipedia 'a pair of terminal lobes hinged at the midrib, forming the trap which is the true leaf'. Fix: 'snaps the two halves of one leaf shut on a fly'.

checks.claim: Stem: shuts in a fraction of a second; digests over several days
checks.note: About a tenth of a second; digestion 5-12 days (Wikipedia: about ten days).

checks.claim: Key: it mainly gets nitrogen, scarce in its soil
checks.note: Prey supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and trace elements; nitrogen is the chief one (up to 30-50% of its nitrogen from prey). Stated right.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'energy its leaves cannot make': carnivory is 'a nutritional supplement rather than a primary energy source'; most energy and carbon from photosynthesis
Wrong choices 'water' and 'oxygen': no source names prey as a water or oxygen source; it grows in wet bogs
Context: still an autotroph; can live without catching a fly; wet boggy ground poor in nitrogen and phosphorus
checks.note: Grokipedia: does not require feeding to survive (fed plants grow faster and live longer). 'Can live' is true.

checks.claim: Stem: naturalists counted fungi as plants for centuries (Linnaeus's Cryptogamia, 1753, into the 20th century); now a kingdom of their own (Whittaker 1969)
Key: fungi, like animals, are heterotrophs that feed on food made by others
Wrong choice 'move about from place to place' / context 'Fungi stay put'
checks.note: Mushrooms and moulds grow in place by spreading hyphae. Only the small aquatic chytrid group has swimming zoospores (reproductive cells). Optional tightening: 'Mushrooms and moulds stay put'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'no stiff outer walls' / context: fungal cell walls are rigid and chitin-based, plant walls cellulose
Wrong choice 'sense the world through nerves': fungi have no nervous system
Context: plants and algae are autotrophs
checks.note: Grade-level generalisation (most plants and algae); fine.

checks.claim: Stem: bread mould spreads with fine threads (hyphae) growing into the slice
checks.note: Moulds are multicellular fungi of branching hyphae; black bread mould's rhizoids anchor it and take up nutrients.

checks.claim: Key: it digests the bread outside itself, then absorbs it
checks.note: Secretes extracellular enzymes (amylases, proteases, pectinases) that break starch into simpler compounds, then absorbs them.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'makes its own food from light' / context: fungi lack chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise
Wrong choice 'feeds on water from the damp air' / context: moisture is the most critical requirement, but water is not its food
checks.note: Mould can take moisture from the air, but its food is organic matter; the lure is a true need misread as food, which is wrong as stated.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'food stored in the spore' / context: the spore holds far too little to feed it
checks.note: Spore reserves (trehalose, mannitol, lipids) fuel only swelling and the first germ tube; outside carbon and nitrogen are needed for hyphal growth.

checks.claim: Context: digestive juices break the bread's starch into simpler food
Stem: a paramecium is a single slipper-shaped cell of pond water
Stem: when it bumps into something it backs up and sets off another way (avoidance reaction)
checks.note: 'rapidly reversing the direction of ciliary beating to back away and reorient'.

checks.claim: Key: it beats thousands of tiny hairs (cilia), in waves
checks.note: 'covered entirely with thousands of short, hair-like cilia'; metachronal waves; up to about 1 mm a second.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'one whip-like tail' / context: that is Euglena's flagellum
checks.note: Euglena has one long emergent flagellum (a second stays short inside the cell).

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'false feet' / context: that is how an amoeba crawls
Wrong choice 'squirts jets of water': its contractile vacuoles expel water only for osmotic balance, not movement
Stem: an amoeba is a single cell of ponds and sediments that eats smaller living things such as bacteria
checks.note: Grokipedia: Amoeba preys on bacteria, algae and other microorganisms; lives in ponds, streams, soils and sediments.

checks.claim: Key: it surrounds the meal and closes it inside (phagocytosis: pseudopods form a food cup that pinches off as a food vacuole)
Wrong choice 'tiny mouth': no mouth or fixed feeding opening; food is taken in wherever the surface encloses it
Wrong choice 'whip-like tail': an amoeba moves and feeds by pseudopodia, no flagellum
Wrong choice 'sticky slime': no source describes an amoeba trapping prey in slime
checks.note: Sticky net-like pseudopodia belong to foraminifera, not the amoeba; slime belongs to slime moulds, a separate group.

checks.claim: Context: pseudopods ('false feet'), food vacuole where the prey is digested

unit_notes: 2 errors, both one-phrase fixes in otherwise sound questions. (1) 3cd6a2cffd context: 'even the longest [muscle cell] is under a third of a metre' is not safe; OpenStax says up to 30 cm, but sartorius fibres are estimated at 35-45 cm and a 2005 J. Neurosci. study found fibres running nearly the full length of a 50 cm muscle; say 'far short of a metre'. (2) 00595305b2 stem: a flytrap's trap is one leaf with two hinged lobes, not 'two leaves'. Checked on request: the stem names the sciatic-nerve neuron's route correctly (1 m, Grokipedia; 'one meter or more', Wikipedia); the red-cell stem says human, so nucleated bird cells do not clash; no Euglena lure is partly true (it can feed in the dark, but never hunts by sight); the flytrap key is nitrogen, not energy, stated right. Optional: 58955065c6 'Fungi stay put' could read 'Mushrooms and moulds stay put' (chytrid zoospores swim).
